## Appendix E Zero temperature numerics for the Bosonic/Fermionic SYK and the Random Rotor models

We consider Dyson-Schwinger equations for the retarded Green’s function for bosonic and fermionic SYK for $q=4$ case, which is obtained by analytic continuation from the Matsubara frequency $i\omega_{n}\to\omega+i0$ . The first Dyson-Schwinger equation reads

$$ \displaystyle G_{R}(\omega)^{-1}=\omega+i0+\mu-\Sigma_{R}(\omega)\,. $$

Here for brevity we don’t explicitly label Green’s functions by index $a=f,\mathfrak{b}$ but we will use symbol $\zeta_{a}$ , which is $\zeta_{f}=-1$ and $\zeta_{\mathfrak{b}}=1$ . In general for the Green’s function and self-energy we define analytic in the upper half plane functions $G(z)$ and $\Sigma(z)$ , which are expressed through the spectral densities $\rho(\omega)$ and $\sigma(\omega)$ as

$$ \displaystyle G(z)=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}d\omega\frac{\rho(\omega)}{z-\omega}\,,\quad\Sigma(z)=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}d\omega\frac{\sigma(\omega)}{z-\omega}\,. $$

The Matsubara and retarded Green’s functions can be obtained from these functions by taking $z=i\omega_{n}$ and $z=\omega+i0$ . We can find the spectral density as $\rho(\omega)=-\frac{1}{\pi}\textrm{Im}G_{R}(\omega)$ . Also using the representation (196) we can obtain Green’s function in imaginary time expressed through integral over the spectral density

$$ \displaystyle G(\tau)=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{n}G(i\omega_{n})e^{-i\omega_{n}\tau}=-\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}d\omega\frac{\rho(\omega)e^{-\omega\tau}}{1-\zeta e^{-\beta\omega}},\quad\tau\in(0,\beta)\,. $$

We notice that $\zeta G(\beta^{-})-G(0^{+})=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}d\omega\rho(\omega)=1$ for arbitrary temperature. To obtain the second Dyson-Schwinger equation for the retarded self-energy $\Sigma_{R}(\omega)$ we consider this equation in the Matsubara space $\Sigma(\tau)=J^{2}G^{2}(\tau)G(\beta-\tau)$ and use (197) to write it through the spectral density

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma(i\omega_{n})=-J^{2}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\prod_{i=1}^{3}(d\omega_{i}\rho(\omega_{i}))\frac{n(\omega_{1})n(\omega_{2})n(-\omega_{3})+n(-\omega_{1})n(-\omega_{2})n(\omega_{3})}{\omega_{1}+\omega_{2}-\omega_{3}-i\omega_{n}}\,, $$

where $n(\omega)=1/(e^{\beta\omega}-\zeta)$ is the Bose or Fermi distribution and we can get $\Sigma_{R}(\omega)=\Sigma(i\omega_{n}=\omega+i0)$ . At zero temperature $\beta=\infty$ we can replace $n_{\mathfrak{b}}(\omega)$ by $-\theta(-\omega)$ and $n_{f}(\omega)$ by $\theta(-\omega)$ . Though $n_{\mathfrak{b}}(\omega)$ is divergent for $\omega\to 0$ , we assume that this divergence does not play any role. Functions $G_{R}(\omega)$ and $\Sigma_{R}(\omega)$ are complex valued and further we will adopt notations for their real and imaginary parts $G_{R}(\omega)=G^{\prime}(\omega)+iG^{\prime\prime}(\omega)$ and $\Sigma_{R}(\omega)=\Sigma^{\prime}(\omega)+i\Sigma^{\prime\prime}(\omega)$ . So for $\beta=\infty$ using (198) we find

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma^{\prime\prime}(\omega)=\begin{cases}\zeta\pi J^{2}\int_{0}^{\omega_{1}+\omega_{2}\leq\omega}d\omega_{1}d\omega_{2}\rho(\omega_{1})\rho(\omega_{2})\rho(\omega_{1}+\omega_{2}-\omega),\quad\omega>0\\
\zeta\pi J^{2}\int^{0}_{\omega_{1}+\omega_{2}\geq\omega}d\omega_{1}d\omega_{2}\rho(\omega_{1})\rho(\omega_{2})\rho(\omega_{1}+\omega_{2}-\omega),\quad\omega<0\,.\end{cases} $$

Below in all formulas we set $J=1$ for brevity. We anticipate that at zero temperature the functions $\rho(\omega)$ and $\Sigma^{\prime\prime}(\omega)$ will have discontinuity. So it will be convenient to use a new set of functions defined separetely for $\omega>0$ and $\omega<0$

$$ \displaystyle\rho(\omega)=\begin{cases}\frac{g_{+}(\omega)}{\sqrt{\omega}},\quad\omega>0\\
\frac{g_{-}(-\omega)}{\sqrt{-\omega}},\quad\omega<0\end{cases}\,,\quad\Sigma^{\prime\prime}(\omega)=\begin{cases}4\pi\sqrt{\omega}s_{+}(\omega),\quad\omega>0\\
4\pi\sqrt{-\omega}s_{-}(-\omega),\quad\omega<0\end{cases}\,. $$

We make change of variables $\omega_{1}=\omega\sin^{2}u\cos^{2}\phi$ and $\omega_{2}=\omega\sin^{2}u\sin^{2}\phi$ in (199) and obtain

$$ \displaystyle s_{\pm}(\omega)=\zeta\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}du\sin u\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}d\phi\;g_{\pm}(\omega\sin^{2}u\cos^{2}\phi)g_{\pm}(\omega\sin^{2}u\sin^{2}\phi)g_{\mp}(\omega\cos^{2}u)\,, $$

and we notice that $s_{\pm}(x)$ and $g_{\pm}(x)$ are defined only for a positive argument. Now it is left to find a real part $\Sigma^{\prime}(\omega)$ of the self-energy. For this we use the Kramers-Kronig relation

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma^{\prime}(\omega) \displaystyle=\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\frac{d\nu}{\pi}\frac{\Sigma^{\prime\prime}(\nu)-\Sigma^{\prime\prime}(\omega)}{\nu-\omega}\,. $$

Defining $\Sigma^{\prime}_{\pm}(\omega)$ as $\Sigma^{\prime}(\omega)=\Sigma^{\prime}_{+}(\omega)\theta(\omega)+\Sigma^{\prime}_{-}(-\omega)\theta(-\omega)$ we find

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma^{\prime}_{\pm}(\omega) \displaystyle=\pm\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{0}^{+\infty}\frac{d\nu}{\pi}\left(\frac{\Sigma^{\prime\prime}_{\pm}(\nu)-\Sigma^{\prime\prime}_{\pm}(\omega)}{\nu-\omega}-\frac{\Sigma^{\prime\prime}_{\mp}(\nu)-\Sigma^{\prime\prime}_{\pm}(\omega)}{\nu+\omega}\right)\,. $$

At zero temperature we set chemical potential $\mu=\Sigma^{\prime}(\omega=0)$ , so introducing $h_{\pm}(\omega)$ as

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma^{\prime}(\omega)-\Sigma^{\prime}(0)=\begin{cases}4\sqrt{\omega}h_{+}(\omega),\quad\omega>0\\
4\sqrt{-\omega}h_{-}(-\omega),\quad\omega<0\end{cases}\, $$

and simplifying expressions we finally obtain

$$ \displaystyle h_{\pm}(\omega)=\pm\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{0}^{+\infty}d\nu\left(\frac{\sqrt{\omega}s_{\pm}(\nu)-\sqrt{\nu}s_{\pm}(\omega)}{\sqrt{\nu}(\nu-\omega)}+\frac{\sqrt{\omega}s_{\mp}(\nu)+\sqrt{\nu}s_{\pm}(\omega)}{\sqrt{\nu}(\nu+\omega)}\right)\,. $$

Now using the first Dyson-Schwinger equation we can get $g_{\pm}$ from $s_{\pm}$ and $h_{\pm}$

$$ \displaystyle g_{\pm}(\omega)=-\frac{4s_{\pm}(\omega)}{(4h_{\pm}(\omega)\mp\sqrt{\omega})^{2}+16\pi^{2}(s_{\pm}(\omega))^{2}}\,. $$

We solve Dyson-Schwinger equations iteratively using (201), (205) and (206) and also imposing the initial conditions coming from the conformal solution (59)

$$ \displaystyle g_{\pm}(0)=\frac{C\sin(\frac{\pi}{4}\pm\theta)}{\pi},\;s_{\pm}(0)=-\frac{\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\pm\theta\right)}{4\pi C},\;h_{\pm}(0)=\mp\frac{\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\pm\theta\right)}{4C},\;C=\Big(\frac{-\zeta\pi}{\cos 2\theta}\Big)^{1/4}\,. $$

We can compute the chemical potential numerically using that $\mu=\Sigma^{\prime}(\omega=0)$ and eq. (203):

$$ \displaystyle\mu=4\int_{0}^{+\infty}d\omega\frac{s_{+}(\omega)-s_{-}(\omega)}{\sqrt{\omega}}\,. $$

In the random rotor model defined in the Section VI the spectral density $\rho(\omega)$ is an odd function due to the particle-hole symmetry. Thus we have $g_{-}(\omega)=-g_{+}(\omega)$ and $s_{-}(\omega)=-s_{+}(\omega)$ , where equation for $s_{+}(\omega)$ is written in (201) ( $\zeta=1$ in this case). Also $h_{-}(\omega)=h_{+}(\omega)$ and from (205) we find

$$ \displaystyle h_{+}(\omega)=\int_{0}^{+\infty}d\nu\frac{2\omega(\sqrt{\omega}s_{+}(\nu)-\sqrt{\nu}s_{+}(\omega))}{\sqrt{\nu}(\nu^{2}-\omega^{2})}\,. $$

The first Schwinger-Dyson equation in the random rotor model reads

$$ \displaystyle g_{+}(\omega)=-\frac{4s_{+}(\omega)}{(\omega^{3/2}-4h_{+}(\omega))^{2}+16\pi^{2}s_{+}(\omega)^{2}}\, $$

and the boundary conditions are obtained from (207) for $\theta=\pi/2$ .
